title: The Odor They Learned to Detect — Unilateral Nostril Androstenone Induction (Mainland 2002), Human OR7D4 Genetic Polymorphisms (Keller 2007) & Olfactory Training

teenKit.tldr: Your genes dictate whether a single steroid molecule smells like sweet vanilla, toxic sweat, or absolutely nothing at all. Even wilder, you can trick your brain into learning new scents through targeted olfactory training.
teenKit.whyItMatters: It proves that reality isn't universal—two people standing in the exact same room can experience fundamentally different sensory universes based entirely on their microscopic DNA receptors.
keyTakeaways: Androstenone is a testosterone-derived steroid that triggers completely opposite reactions in different people, ranging from floral sweetness to stale urine.
A massive chunk of the human population cannot smell androstenone at all because of specific genetic variations in their olfactory receptors.
Olfactory plasticity means your nose and brain aren't hardwired forever; with deliberate exposure training, you can actually learn to detect and process scents you previously missed.

vocab.meaning: A steroid compound found in sweat and pork that smells totally different to different people depending on their genetics.
A specific protein sensor in your nose that determines how intensely you perceive certain steroid smells.
The scientific phenomenon where training one side of your body or sensory system somehow teaches the untrained opposite side.
The brain and nose's ability to rewire and adapt their sense of smell over time through repeated exposure.

quiz.question: When multiple people sniff a bottle of androstenone in a controlled lab setting, what happens?
options: Everyone agrees it smells like vanilla.
Their reactions violently diverge, smelling anything from sweet floral to foul urine or nothing at all.
Everyone immediately experiences a headache from the high toxicity.
quiz.explanation: Genetic variations cause human perception of androstenone to split into three radically different sensory experiences.

quiz.question: What does the OR7D4 gene variant directly control in human biology?
options: How your body processes testosterone into muscle mass.
How intensely and what valence (pleasant or foul) you assign to certain meat and sweat odors.
The physical size and shape of your external nostrils.
How fast your brain clears air through a vacuum hood.
quiz.explanation: OR7D4 genetic polymorphisms act as the primary molecular switch governing how we experience specific steroid odors.

quiz.question: Why did researchers use a sterile room with an automated voice and a vacuum hood in the Mainland experiment?
options: To save money on hiring human lab assistants.
To completely strip away visual bias, context, and environmental noise so they could isolate pure olfactory data.
To test if human subjects could survive in an airtight space capsule.
To prevent the chemical androstenone from exploding.
quiz.explanation: Isolating the variable of smell required removing every possible external cue or sensory distraction.
